body_markdown:
## Executive Insight


In this work, researchers aimed to address the negative impact of maltitol on yogurt fermentation. Through several investigations, they found that sucrose transport plays a role in maltitol-mediated growth inhibition of *S. thermophilus* . They also showed that bioengineering starter cultures could improve industrial dairy fermentation.


## Why This Research Matters


Sugar reduction is a key trend in the global[dairy](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/) industry. Consumers, the industry and regulators are pressuring for the reduction of this one.


Maltitol is widely used as a sucrose alternative in yogurt and other fermented[dairy](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/) products. However, researchers observed that maltitol can significantly delay yogurt fermentation. It inhibits the growth of Streptococcus thermophilus, a critical starter culture species. This research identified the sucrose phosphotransferase system as a major contributor to this inhibitory effect. It also showed that disruption of this pathway renders strains insensitive to maltitol.


As a results, these findings provide new insights into the interactions between sweeteners and starter cultures. This research also offers practical strategies to improve fermentation performance in reduced-sugar[dairy](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/dairy/) products.


Furthermore, this research demonstrates that the use of maltitol as a selective screening tool enables the development of sucrose-negative starter cultures. In addition, it supports the design of next-generation cultures with improved fermentation robustness and better post-acidification control.

IFF Expert Contributors[Haiyun Wen](https://www.iff.com/experts/haiyun-wen/) and **[Rongkai Guo](https://www.iff.com/experts/rongkai-guo/) ,** among others, contributed to this research.


## Practical Applications in Food Biosciences


These findings provide new insights into the interactions between sweeteners and starter cultures. They also offer practical strategies for improving fermentation performance in reduced-sugar dairy products. Furthermore, the use of maltitol as a selective screening tool enables the development of sucrose-negative starter cultures, supporting the design of next-generation cultures with improved fermentation robustness and better post-acidification control.


## How This Research Was Conducted


This research combined microbiological, genetic, and fermentation-based approaches to investigate the impact of maltitol on yogurt starter cultures.


- First, a collection of Streptococcus thermophilus strains was screened to assess growth performance in medium containing maltitol.


- Next, they conducted fermentation trials to evaluate the effect of maltitol on acidification kinetics and yogurt production performance. To identify the genetic basis of strain-dependent responses, comparative genomic analyses were performed between maltitol-sensitive and maltitol-insensitive strains.


- Researches then validate candidate genes through genetic characterization and phenotypic assessment.


- In addition, they compared growth behavior, carbohydrate utilization, and fermentation performance to confirm the role of the identified pathway.


- Finally, by integrating microbial physiology, genomics, and[dairy fermentation](https://www.iff.com/food-beverage/food-bioscience/cultures/dairy-cultures/fresh-fermented/) studies, the work established a mechanistic link between maltitol sensitivity and sucrose transport metabolism. These results provided practical insights for starter culture selection and the development of robust cultures for reduced-sugar dairy applications.
